newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Car sales in low gear ahead of UK show.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Car sales in low gear ahead of UK show.

text.p: Fresh from banging the sales drum at the Paris Motor Show, international car makers were gearing up for the next big showcase - the seventy-first British International Motor Show which kicks off on Tuesday next week.

The British show in Birmingham will be host to more than 200 international exhibitors including volume giants like Ford, General Motors' UK manufacturer Vauxhall as well as luxury car maker BMW and its UK arm Rover.
The organisers, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders said that the market backdrop was a tough one, with most of the UK growth stemming from company sales.
Sales to the general public remained sluggish, said Graham Dynott of the SMMT.
"The main concern in this country isn't that sales are not going up. They were up four percent last year. But the private individual is not going to the showroom, he's staying away."
Instead sales had been growing in the company sector. "Fleet sales are moving ahead. But we are not able to persuade Joe Public to visit car showrooms," Dynott told Reuters.
The wider European market is suffering from a squeeze on margins as manufacturers chase market share in a tighter sales environment.
Consequently overall sales might be up but margins are down, said Colin Whitbread, consultant with London's Economist Intelligence Unit.
"(European) volumes are up five or six percent, but operating performance has been going downhill," he told Reuters.
"The companies are selling more cars and making less and less from each unit. They are selling the cars but they are having to give away more to move the metal."
Customers want keen pricing but also the added extras which are now available due to advances in technology.
Competition means items like air-bags and stereos are no longer extras, but part of the package.
In the UK, new car registrations were up 3.96 percent on last year for the first nine months of 1996.
That compares with the a low point in 1991, when registrations fell 21 percent on the previous year. Since then sales in the UK car market have gradually recovered.
New car registrations for the whole of 1996 are projected to be 2.01 million, with 2.05 million projected for 1997.
The high point for car production was in the mid-1960s, according to SMMT figures, when 1.9 million units were produced.
The figure last year was 1.5 million. However, that total was dominated by exports, whereas in the mid-sixties the industry was led by the domestic market.
